title: Angels (CCC 328–336)
hook: spiritual creatures, messengers, and a guardian beside each person

segments.voice: Yesterday, why evil: the hard question, and the Catechism's honest answer that no quick answer will do. Your line was no quick answer. Did you show up for someone? Today, day three hundred, and some company for the road. Day three hundred.

Angels are everywhere in our culture. Chubby babies with harps on greeting cards. Women in white robes on top of Christmas trees. People say someone who died has become an angel now. A sweet kid gets called an angel. Almost none of that is what the Catholic Church actually teaches about angels. What it does teach is stranger, and in a way more comforting: that you have never, for one moment of your life, been completely alone. Today: angels.
screen: `HARPS, ROBES, CHRISTMAS TREES.` → `NOT WHAT THE CHURCH TEACHES.` → `NEVER COMPLETELY ALONE.`

segments.voice: First, the word. Angel comes from the Greek angelos, messenger. Augustine made a sharp point about it, and the Catechism repeats it: angel is the name of their job, not their nature. What they are is spirit. What they do is carry God's messages. Think of Gabriel at Nazareth, telling Mary she would bear a son. Second, what they are. The Catechism, from paragraph 328, says the existence of angels is a truth of faith. They are purely spiritual creatures, with intelligence and will, personal and immortal. And they're created. They are not God, and, despite the greeting cards, they're not people who died. When someone you love dies, Catholics pray they're with God, but they don't become angels. Third, the guardian. Jesus says, in Matthew, in the Douay-Rheims: "See that you despise not one of these little ones: for I say to you, that their angels in heaven always see the face of my Father who is in heaven." And a psalm promises: "For he hath given his angels charge over thee; to keep thee in all thy ways." The Catechism says that from infancy to death, human life is surrounded by the angels' watchful care, and quotes Saint Basil: beside each believer stands an angel as protector and shepherd. Fourth, never alone. Catholics keep the feast of the Guardian Angels on October 2, and many children learn a short prayer to their guardian angel before they learn almost anything else. It's a small, steady comfort: on the dark nights, in the hospital hallway, on the drive home, someone God sent is keeping watch.
screen: `ANGELOS — MESSENGER.` · `SPIRITS, NOT PEOPLE WHO DIED.` · `AN ANGEL BESIDE EACH BELIEVER.` · `THE FEAST OF OCTOBER 2.` · then, large: `TO KEEP THEE IN ALL THY WAYS.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: the guardian angel prayer. It's the one many Catholic children learn first. Angel of God, my guardian dear, to whom God's love commits me here, ever this day be at my side, to light and guard, to rule and guide. Amen. If you pray, say it once, slowly, on your own. If you don't, sit with the idea for a minute: that someone might be keeping watch beside you, right now. Notice how that feels. The bell holds the time.
Angel. From the Greek for messenger: a spiritual creature made by God, and in Catholic belief, a guardian beside each person. Today's word.
Your line: never alone. Three hundred days on the path. Today, in one lonely moment, remember the promise: someone is keeping watch. Day three hundred.

howItsDone: Catholics keep the feast of the Holy Guardian Angels on October 2 and of the archangels Michael, Gabriel and Raphael on September 29, and many families teach children the guardian angel prayer at bedtime.
